extracted.intended_audience: young authors, poets, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical stylistic and compositional guidance for poets, dramatists, and prose writers on diction, imagery, adaptation of rules to ends, and expectations about public reception. Emphasises how lines should read on the page as well as how they fare in performance and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for admission of double epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for the admission of double epithets seems to be this: either that they should be already denizens of our language, such as blood-stained, terror-stricken, self-applauding: or when a new epithet, or one found in books only, is hazarded, that it, at least, be one word, not two words made one by mere virtue of the printers hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow double epithets only when they are established compounds (blood-stained, terror-stricken) or when a new epithet is presented as a single word rather than two words joined by a hyphen. English (being almost without cases) is unfitted for many compounds; if a compound suggests itself, seek another way to express the sense — chances favour finding a better single word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid phrasing translatable into simpler words
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is translatable in other and simpler words of the same language, without loss of sense or dignity, is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler expressions when they do not sacrifice meaning or 'dignity' (where 'dignity' = absence of ludicrous and debasing associations). If a phrase can be rendered in plainer wording without loss, the more complex original is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain ends before you apply rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics are too apt to forget, that rules are but means to an end; consequently, where the ends are different, the rules must be likewise so. We must have ascertained what the end is, before we can determine what the rules ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mechanically apply formal or historical rules (e.g., classical dramatic prescriptions) without first determining the artistic ends of the work. Rules should be adapted to the purpose and circumstances of the drama/poem, not imposed regardless of differing aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate passages by their collective meaning, not isolated felicities
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers receive pleasure from separate images and phrases successively, without asking themselves whether the collective meaning was sense or nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing, ensure that pleasing individual lines or images cohere to produce a clear collective meaning. Avoid sequences of attractive phrases that collectively convey an absurd or incoherent idea. Analyse passages sentence-by-sentence but always test the whole for sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and inconsistent metaphors that destroy the visual likeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more simple as a description, or more accurate as a simile... Now here -- (not to mention the tremendous bombast) -- the Dog Star, so called, is turned into a real dog, a very odd dog, a fire, fever, plague, and death-breathing, red, air-tainting dog: and the whole visual likeness is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep metaphors consistent with their visual image; do not exaggerate or translate a simile in a way that sacrifices the original visual likeness and makes the image absurd. Avoid grandiose language ('bombast') that breaks the intended comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chastity of diction and harmony of verse are critical virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: In chastity of diction however, and the harmony of blank verse, Cowper leaves Thomson immeasurably below him; yet still I feel the latter to have been the born poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value clear, restrained diction and the aural harmony of verse (especially blank verse). Even when comparing poets of different temperaments, prioritize purity of language and smooth metrical/harmonic execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poems should be able to stand when read, not only when recited by a performer
rubrics_metrics.description: It is equally possible, though not equally common, that a reader left to himself should sink below the poem, as that the poem left to itself should flag beneath the feelings of the reader... the enkindling reciter, by perpetual comment of looks and tones, lends his own will and apprehensive faculty to his auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose so that the work communicates when encountered quietly on the page; avoid relying solely on a charismatic performer to lend meaning or force. Beware of pieces that succeed only in performance and not in the text itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate differences between private recitation praise and public printed reception
rubrics_metrics.description: In their calculations on the probable reception of a poem, they must subtract to a large amount from the panegyric, which may have encouraged them to publish it... allowances must be made for private enmity... the necessity of a certain proportion of abuse and ridicule in a Review... and... the excitement and temporary sympathy of feeling, which the recitation of the poem by an admirer... calls forth in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage expectations: admiration in private circles or during recitation often does not translate to printed success. Consider the roles of private enmity, commercialized ridicule, and performative sympathy when predicting reception; do not overvalue oral panegyric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure suitability of lines to medium and audience (e.g., stage vs. page)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a dramatic poem... occurred the following passage... (critic) here come Coleridge’s metaphysics! ... the very same motive (that is, not that the lines were unfit for the present state of our immense theatres; but that they were metaphysics) was assigned elsewhere for the rejection...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for a specific medium (theatre, public recitation, private reading), ensure the diction, subject-matter, and mode of exposition fit that medium's expectations and constraints. Lines deemed 'metaphysical' or otherwise unsuitable for the theatre may be rejected regardless of their intrinsic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of personal gossip and the effects of literary personality-culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially in this age of personality, this age of literary and political gossiping... when the most vapid satires have become the objects of a keen public interest, purely from the number of contemporary characters named...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that literary reputation and reception are often influenced by gossip, satire, and personality-culture rather than pure literary quality. Take precautions about how personal associations or topical notes may colour critical response.
